The math drills gauge prints today 0/40 on weekends, which reads as a fault (it triggered a false-alarm investigation, F-0865/J-0624). school.py has SCHOOL_WEEKDAYS_ONLY=True, so on Saturday/Sunday the gauge should say school closed (weekend) instead of a zero count, and on weekdays it should note whether Du was awake during the 09:45-10:30 maths period before implying a miss.

No amend/retract subcommand: a finding found partly wrong (F-0887's 'no callers' half, corrected by F-0888) can only be superseded by a new finding; readers of F-0887 alone never learn it was corrected. Backtick-in-double-quotes command substitution (the documented F-0840 footgun) recurred 2026-09-05 (J-0532/F-0894): a --evidence string included a markdown-style code-quoted 'git log --follow -- core/thermal.py' for readability, and since the Bash tool runs a real POSIX shell, the backticks executed it for real and spliced the full multi-commit git log output into the stored evidence field (harmless this time -- git log is read-only -- but the same class of bug that booted a duplicate live process in F-0840 if the quoted text had been a mutating command). Suggest: findings_log.py/decide.py/job_queue.py/idea_log.py all accept a --claim-file/--evidence-file/--briefing-file alternative that reads the text from a file instead of a shell arg, so a session can Write the string to a scratch file and never pass long freeform text (with quotes, backticks, $, etc.) through the shell at all. This would close the whole class of shell-metacharacter footguns these long-text CLI args are exposed to, not just backticks.
resolved_why: Duplicate -- filed without --session by mistake (tool warned on the call), re-filed correctly as S-0044 with --session so it shows up in this session's rollup. See S-0044 for the actual suggestion content.

text: Provenance-tracking gap noticed while working J-0517: F-0705 (findings.jsonl, 2026-09-02) records 'spawned_jobs': ['J-0521'], but J-0521 itself (job_queue.jsonl) records 'source': 'finding:F-0717' and 'spawned_from': {'type':'finding','id':'F-0717'} -- a DIFFERENT, later finding about an unrelated topic (social/symbolic kind budget, not F-0705's episodic-kind-saturation topic). Either a job's source/spawned_from got overwritten by a later spawn call reusing the same job id, or a finding's spawned_jobs list can point at a job that was later repurposed without updating the finding's own record. Either way, F-0705's own follow-up thread was silently orphaned -- nothing currently tracks it, and a future reader trusting F-0705.spawned_jobs would land on the wrong job entirely. Worth checking whether job_queue.py's spawn command can ever be called again against an id already claimed by a prior spawn (should be append-only, one id per spawn), and whether findings_log.py's spawn-job could cross-check that the target job's own source still points back at the calling finding before treating the link as valid.

F-0918 (2026-09-05): Workflow-spawned agents in a job-run batch all share ONE physical scratchpad directory -- the top-level orchestrating session's own UUID path -- not individually isolated ones per agent. Confirmed live: job J-0559's agent and job J-0621's agent (unrelated jobs, same 15-agent batch) both independently wrote a scratch script named record_finding.py to the identical path 0.5s apart, and the second write silently clobbered the first on disk (caught only because J-0621 had already executed its own copy before being overwritten). Fix: job-run's own dispatch prompt template (the tier2Prompt/tier3Prompt/housekeepingPrompt functions in its Workflow skeleton) should tell each dispatched agent to name any scratch script it writes with its own job id in the filename (e.g. record_finding_J-0621.py, not record_finding.py) -- a one-line addition to the ground rules block, since the collision is entirely about filename choice, not about needing real per-agent directory isolation from the harness.
resolved_why: Added step 10 to job-run's SKILL.md ('What you must do when invoked'), mirroring step 9's git-rule pattern: every dispatched prompt, all tiers, must tell the agent to qualify any scratch filename with its own job id (e.g. record_finding_J-0621.py, not record_finding.py), since a Workflow batch's agents share one physical scratchpad directory, not isolated ones per agent. Added a matching '2026-09-05 scratchpad-collision finding' section citing F-0918's cross-checked transcript evidence (J-0559 wrote record_finding.py at 09:03:38.109Z; J-0621 got an edited_text_file notification on the same path 0.499s later), consistent with the file's existing incident-documentation style.

text: Provenance mismatch found while working J-0642 (confirmed via job_queue.py show / findings_log.py show, not just paraphrased): F-0705's own record carries "spawned_jobs": ["J-0521"], but J-0521's own record carries "source": "finding:F-0717" and "spawned_from": {"type": "finding", "id": "F-0717"} -- a DIFFERENT, later finding about an unrelated topic (social/symbolic kind weight, not F-0705's episodic-saturation-is-log-noise claim). So F-0705's own follow-up thread was silently orphaned: nothing actually spawned from F-0705 is tracked anywhere, and a reader trusting F-0705.spawned_jobs would be pointed at the wrong finding's follow-up. Nothing in job_queue.py's spawn or findings_log.py's spawn-job path appears to cross-check that a finding's own spawned_jobs list and the resulting job's own source/spawned_from agree at write time. Worth either a write-time assertion (spawn-job should fail loudly if it's about to record a spawned_jobs entry that won't match the new job's own source) or a read-time consistency check (plan-schema-audit or a similar sweep already exists for plan-doc gaps; this is the analogous check for job<->finding cross-references) that surfaces existing mismatches like this one across the whole ledger, not just the one instance found here by hand.

decide.py open's plan-slug validator (line ~106, 'is not a real plan slug (checked docs/plans/ and docs/staged/)') only scans docs/plans/ and docs/staged/, but at least one real, heavily-referenced plan doc -- docs/memory_levels_plan.md, the single most-linked plan in the whole project per MEMORY.md's own '[Memory Levels (RANKED #1)]' entry -- lives directly under docs/, not in either subdirectory. 6 prior decisions (D-0072, D-0089, D-0091, D-0092, D-0116, D-0124) already reference plan="memory_levels_plan" successfully (opened before this check existed or tightened, or opened with --force without saying so), so this is an established real slug, not a typo -- but a plain `decide open --plan memory_levels_plan` today (tried live during J-0642) is refused as 'not a real plan slug' and requires --force to proceed, which is easy to mistake for 'this plan doesn't really exist, maybe I have the wrong slug' the first time you hit it. Either (a) have the validator also check docs/*.md directly (one level, not recursive, to stay cheap), or (b) if docs/ root is meant to be a deliberately-invalid location per the CLAUDE.md staged/plans convention, move memory_levels_plan.md into docs/plans/ (it is clearly graduated, not staged -- Status line says 'Phase 0 + Phase 1 BUILT & LIVE') and note that migration in the plan's own Current State so the next person doesn't wonder why the file moved.

Noticed while auditing D-0137 follow-through: job_queue.py spawn --from finding:F-0786 produced J-0573 with source/spawned_from correctly pointing at F-0786, but F-0786s own findings.jsonl record still shows spawned_jobs: [] (findings_log.py spawn-job writes both sides of that link; job_queue.py spawn --from finding:X apparently only writes the jobs side). Not fixed here -- flagging per CLAUDE.md rule 5, out of scope for the job (J-0591) this was noticed during.

SKILL.md should warn against backtick-quoted command citations inside a --claim/--evidence string passed via the Bash tool with double quotes: backticks execute for real (command substitution) instead of staying literal text. This is now a CONFIRMED SECOND occurrence (F-0840 booted a duplicate live Du process; this session, F-0937, spliced a live test re-run stdout into an evidence field and silently blanked two other citations whose backtick-wrapped commands failed). The same risk applies to every sibling tool with free-text CLI args (job_queue.py, decide.py, idea_log.py), not just findings_log.py -- worth a shared warning, e.g. in each SKILL.md or a CLAUDE.md ground rule: use single-quoted Bash strings for --claim/--evidence/--briefing/--ruling/etc, or write plain text without backticks, never double-quoted-with-backticks.
resolved_why: The structural fix (S-0044, applied same pass) supersedes a documentation-only warning: every free-text CLI arg across findings_log.py/decide.py/job_queue.py/idea_log.py/thought_log.py/skill_manager.py now has a --*-file alternative that never touches a shell argument at all, so the backtick-in-double-quotes footgun is avoided by construction rather than by remembering a quoting rule. Also added the warning this suggestion asked for anyway, as job-run's SKILL.md step 11 plus a dated incident note citing all four real occurrences (F-0840/F-0894/F-0937/F-0938), so a session reading the runbook sees both the rule and the tool that makes following it easy.

text: No verb exists to mark an EXISTING ready/in_progress job as blocked-on-a-decision once real work surfaces that it needs founder input mid-flight (only add/spawn/start/done exist -- add/spawn set autonomy=needs_input only on a NEW job). J-0592 hit this directly: started as a plain build job, then a fresh decision (D-0174) turned up mid-work that the build itself now hinges on. The only way to reflect that today is prose in a finding + a plan-doc note, leaving the job itself sitting in_progress with nothing in job_queue.py show itself signalling why, or that it differs from an in_progress job that's just slow. A small 'job_queue.py block J-XXXX --decision D-YYYY --reason ...' (flips autonomy to needs_input and stamps a blocked_on field, still leaving status in_progress) would make this visible to job-queue next/list without a human having to cross-reference a finding by hand.

job_queue.py's "add" subcommand has --isolation {none,required}, but neither "spawn" (job_queue.py) nor "spawn-job" (findings_log.py) exposes that flag -- a job created via either spawn path always defaults to isolation:none even when its briefing clearly requires isolation (e.g. J-0663, spawned from F-0950, touches data/subconscious_state.json's tension centroids; I had to write "ISOLATION REQUIRED" into the free-text briefing as the only available mitigation, rather than the structured field the rest of the toolchain -- and this very batch's own runbook -- reads to decide isolation policy up front). Suggest adding --isolation {none,required} to both spawn commands, mirroring "add".

job_run.py's structural hold pre-check (_decision_flags/_is_hold) has two real gaps, both confirmed by reading the source directly (see F-0952): (1) _decision_flags() only matches a decide.py row to a job by the job's own `plan` field or its `spawned_from` decision id -- a decision that lives on a DIFFERENT plan (e.g. D-0016 is tagged peer_correspondence_plan but gates social_world_school.md's Item 1, and is referenced only in that plan doc's prose, not as any job's spawned_from) is never surfaced, for any job, ever. (2) _is_hold() classifies a ruling as an active hold only if its text literally starts with the word "Hold" -- a completely natural founder phrasing like "Not yet, hold -- don't build X right now" fails this check even though it is unambiguously a hold to a human reader. Together these let D-0016's standing "Not yet, hold -- don't build Item 1 or run the behavioral check right now" ruling (made 2026-08-23, never reopened) go undetected by every batch's start-of-batch snapshot across nine job iterations in the social_world_school/peer_correspondence_plan chain, including this one (J-0606). Suggest: (a) _is_hold() should match on the word "hold" appearing anywhere in the first few words of the ruling, not strictly as the first token -- or better, decide.py itself should support/encourage an explicit structured field (e.g. a `status: hold` flag set via `decide.py rule --hold`) instead of relying on ruling-text prefix conventions at all; (b) _decision_flags() should also check, for the job's own plan doc, whether its markdown text cross-references any decision id from ANOTHER plan (a cheap regex for D-\d{4} tokens already exists in other tools like build_edges.py) and include those in the same matching pass, not just same-plan/spawned_from matches.

job_queue.py's own generic `spawn --from finding:F-XXXX` (the exact call this project's own CLAUDE.md job-queue runbook step 10 models: "python job_queue.py spawn --kind ... --from plan:<slug>|decision:D-XXXX ...") does NOT append the new job's id back into that finding's own `spawned_jobs` list -- only findings_log.py's OWN `spawn-job <id>` subcommand does that (it calls the same jq.spawn_record() job-creation helper, then additionally does `rec["spawned_jobs"].append(job["id"]); save(finding_rows)`). Concretely hit on J-0604: I ran `job_queue.py spawn --from finding:F-0949 ...` (creating J-0665, correctly recorded with `spawned_from: {type: finding, id: F-0949}` on the JOB side) then found F-0949's own `spawned_jobs` field still empty. By the time I noticed, findings_log.py spawn-job could no longer be used to fix it without creating a SECOND duplicate job (it always creates a fresh job, no idempotency/link-only mode) -- so the finding-side back-link for J-0665 is now a real, unfixable-without-a-duplicate gap. Suggest one of: (1) job_queue.py's own spawn command detects a `--from finding:F-XXXX` source and appends the new job id into that finding's spawned_jobs list too (mirroring findings_log.py spawn-job's own behavior, so the two code paths produce the same bidirectional link regardless of which tool a session reaches for), or (2) add a lightweight `findings_log.py link-job <finding-id> <job-id>` command that only appends an EXISTING job id to spawned_jobs (no new job creation), for exactly this after-the-fact repair case, or (3) at minimum, have CLAUDE.md's own job-queue runbook / job_queue.py's spawn --help text warn that `--from finding:F-XXXX` should route through findings_log.py spawn-job instead if the finding-side link matters, since the runbook's own step 10 wording (which names plan:/decision: sources, not finding:) makes it easy to reach for the wrong tool when the source actually is a finding.

The Workflow dispatch skeleton's agent prompts (Tier1 template ~line 189, and TIER3_PROMPT per line 207-209) tell every dispatched agent to "Find your own session id from your scratchpad directory path." F-0918 already established that all agents in one Workflow batch share ONE physical scratchpad directory, not an isolated one per agent -- so every concurrently dispatched agent in a batch derives the IDENTICAL session id and all their job_queue.py/findings_log.py/decide.py/idea_log.py calls collapse into one shared session in docs/session_events.jsonl. Confirmed live in this exact 2026-09-05/06 batch (F-0954): session "2e890af5-c14a-40b2-a59c-db0f7731a874" carries 251+ rows spanning multiple unrelated jobs (J-0593, J-0598, J-0604, ...) from clearly different agents. This defeats the per-session rollup --session exists for. Suggest: the orchestrating Workflow script should mint a fresh UUID per dispatched agent call (e.g. crypto.randomUUID() in the script, which DOES have filesystem/JS access even though job_run.py itself doesn't) and interpolate it into each agent(...) prompt as an explicit "your session id is <uuid>" instead of telling the agent to self-derive one from a path now known to be shared.
resolved_why: Applied job-run's own runbook fix (see S-0056's resolution) rather than this suggestion's specific crypto.randomUUID() mechanism: minting fresh randomness inside a Workflow script conflicts with the same determinism-for-resume contract that already blocks Math.random()/Date.now() there (a re-run resuming from cache would mint a DIFFERENT uuid than the cached run used, breaking the very attribution this is meant to fix, even if the runtime doesn't explicitly block crypto.randomUUID() the way it blocks Math.random()). Job ids are already unique, already known to the orchestrator at prompt-build time, and require zero randomness -- baked directly into each command string as --session <job-id>, they solve the identical problem this suggestion identified without the resume-safety risk.

text:
Every subagent a job-run Workflow dispatches receives the ORCHESTRATOR's own scratchpad directory, not a fresh one of its own (F-0918, confirmed again by F-0955). Runbooks currently instruct each dispatched subagent to "find your own session id (the UUID segment in your scratchpad directory path)" and pass it as --session to job_queue.py/findings_log.py/decide.py/idea_log.py -- but since that path is the orchestrator's, EVERY subagent in EVERY batch that orchestrator ever dispatches ends up passing the IDENTICAL --session value. F-0918 only flagged the scratch-FILENAME collision half of this (fixed via job-id-qualified filenames); F-0955 shows the same root cause also comingles every subagent's mutating-call attribution in docs/session_events.jsonl under one session id, for the orchestrating session's whole lifetime -- so a later session_handoff.py rollup --session-id <that id> or /session-wrap silently returns a mass of unrelated subagents' actions, not one coherent session's narrative, with no error or signal that anything is wrong.

Suggested direction: stop deriving --session from the scratchpad path in a dispatched-subagent runbook. Each subagent already has a genuinely unique identifier handed to it directly: its own job id (e.g. "J-0596"). Have the runbook template pass something derived from THAT (e.g. "job:J-0596", or a fresh uuid4 generated once at the top of the subagent's own run and reused for all its own calls) as --session instead, so job_queue.py/findings_log.py/decide.py/idea_log.py all end up attributing a batch subagent's calls to that subagent alone. This needs a decision on the exact scheme (job-id-based vs freshly generated), but the current scheme (shared orchestrator path) is confirmed broken for attribution, not just for scratch files.
resolved_why: Fixed by removing session-derivation from the dispatched-agent runbook entirely, per this suggestion's own job-id-based option: job-run's SKILL.md now bakes --session <job-id> directly into every job-queue/findings-log/decide/idea-log command string TIER1/TIER3_PROMPT generate (e.g. --session J-0621), since the orchestrator already knows each job's id at prompt-build time -- there is nothing left for the agent to derive or get wrong. Confirmed --session's format is unvalidated everywhere it's consumed (log_event, session_handoff.py's rollup filter are both plain string equality), so a job id works as well as a UUID and is more readable in the event log. Added a dated 2026-09-06 section to SKILL.md documenting the fix and citing both this and S-0055.

job_queue.py's `spawn` subcommand has no `--isolation` override (only `add` does) -- `--kind test`/`lab_experiment` always force `isolation=required` via `_ISOLATION_DEFAULT`. This is right for a job that should run in lab_env.py's DB-copy sandbox, but wrong for a "kind": "test" job whose actual task is dogfooding a live-dispatch mechanism against real concurrent usage (real example: J-0669, spawned from J-0590/D-0118, whose whole point is to use the new git-worktree isolation in an ACTUAL job-run batch -- lab_env.py isolation does not apply and would be a wrong first step for whoever picks it up). Worked around this time by leaving the isolation flag as-is and writing the briefing text to make the real intent unambiguous, but `spawn` should accept an `--isolation` override the same way `add` already does, so this class of "kind test but not a lab_env-style test" job does not have to carry a misleading flag.

decide.py's `open`/`rule` and job_queue.py's `add`/`spawn` all take a `--plan` field that plan-index/plan-liveness/memory-links treat as a Du plan-doc slug, but there is no dedicated value for a decision/job that is genuinely about this Claude Code toolchain itself (job-run, job-queue, the plan-index family) rather than about any Du plan. Real example found while working J-0590: D-0118 (job-run git-worktree dispatch) is tagged `plan=actions_manager_overhaul` purely because the session that opened it was mid-way through an actions_manager_overhaul job at the time and reused its current --plan value for an unrelated meta-tooling observation -- its own source finding F-0649 shows the more honest `plan=null` for the same underlying observation. A `--plan _toolchain` (or `--plan none` made explicit rather than only achievable by omitting the flag) convention, with plan-index/plan-liveness special-casing it as "not a Du plan, skip the plan-doc-Current-State-update step", would stop this class of decision/job from either polluting an unrelated plan doc's Current State (this job's own runbook step 9 would otherwise have injected job-run dispatch mechanics into actions_manager_overhaul.md) or silently defaulting to null with no positive signal that null was deliberate.

plan_sync_check.py's own --help/--session text still says "your session id (UUID segment of your scratchpad directory path)" -- exactly the derivation method that job_queue.py/findings_log.py/decide.py/idea_log.py/thought_log.py were fixed away from on 2026-09-06 (F-0954/F-0955) precisely because every agent in one Workflow batch shares the same physical scratchpad directory, so deriving from it silently merges every concurrent agent's plan-sync check_run under one identical id instead of attributing each to its own job/session. Ran into this directly on J-0671 (a batch job): had to skip --session entirely on plan_sync_check.py to avoid contributing to a merged rollup, which means the check_run doesn't show up in any session's `session_handoff.py rollup --session-id <id>` at all per the tool's own warning message. Worth either (a) updating plan_sync_check.py's --help text and rollup-key convention to accept a real job id like "J-0671" the same way the four fixed tools now do, or (b) explicitly documenting that plan_sync_check.py's --session is only meaningful for a single-agent (non-batch) session and should be omitted inside a job-queue/job-run batch.

Noticed while executing J-0669 (whose generic Tier-3 dispatch template, mirroring job-run/SKILL.md
step 6, says unconditionally: "If the job's source names a decision and it is NOT under an active
Hold, rule it: decide.py rule D-XXXX ..."). J-0669's named decision, D-0118, turned out to already
carry a real founder ruling (ruled 2026-09-04, by=travis, a substantive ruling text, not a Hold). Read
decide.py's cmd_rule source directly (lines 131-152): it has NO guard against re-ruling an
already-ruled decision. It pushes the existing ruling/defeater/ruled/by into rec["history"] and then
unconditionally overwrites the top-level ruling/defeater/ruled/by/ruled_session fields with the new
call's values -- so a Tier-3 agent that followed the generic template literally (as I nearly did)
would have called `decide.py rule D-0118 --by claude ...`, silently demoting Travis's own founder
ruling into a nested history array and replacing the decision's top-level "by" with "claude" on a
decision the founder had already settled. This is exactly the class of misattribution CLAUDE.md's own
rule already warns about in the other direction ("a ruling made by Claude is never recorded as the
founder's") -- decide.py's own code has no structural check preventing the same class of corruption
here. Two independent fixes worth considering, either would close this: (a) decide.py's cmd_rule
could refuse (or require an explicit --amend/--reruling flag) when rec["ruling"] is already non-null
and rec["by"] == "travis", the same way cmd_rule already refuses outright on a missing defeater; (b)
job-run/SKILL.md step 6 (and any generic Tier-3 dispatch template built from it) could add an explicit
"check decide.py show D-XXXX first -- if it already has a real (non-Claude) ruling, do not call rule
again; record your new evidence via findings-log with --decision D-XXXX instead" branch, the same way
step 6 already has an explicit active-Hold branch. I did not call decide.py rule on D-0118 for this
reason and used findings_log.py record --decision D-0118 instead -- flagging the gap rather than
silently working around it, since fixing decide.py's own guard logic is out of this job's scope.

plan_sync_check.py's own --help text for --session still says "your session id (UUID segment of your scratchpad directory path)" -- this is the exact derive-from-shared-scratchpad-path approach the 2026-09-06 F-0954/F-0955 fix found buggy (every agent in one Workflow batch shares one physical scratchpad dir, so deriving from it merges concurrent agents' attribution). J-0665's own ground rules explicitly override this for job_queue.py/findings_log.py/decide.py/idea_log.py ("your session value is literally the job id, do not derive it"), but plan_sync_check.py's help text was not updated to match and would mislead an agent who trusts it literally. job_queue.py's cmd_start/cmd_done have no idempotency/state check: `start <id>` unconditionally sets status="in_progress" and overwrites `started` with now(), and `done <id>` unconditionally sets status="done" and overwrites `done_at`, regardless of the job's current status. Hit this live on J-0680: a concurrent/earlier run had already correctly completed it (status=done, started/done_at timestamps real) before I got to it. Calling `start J-0680` again as my own step 2 would have silently discarded the real historical started timestamp and flipped a correctly-done job back to in_progress with no warning; calling `done` again after would just re-stamp done_at with a later, wrong time and emit a duplicate job_done event for the same ref. I avoided both calls once I noticed via `show`, but a less careful agent (or a batch dispatcher that always runs `start` before checking `show`) would not. Suggest: `cmd_start`/`cmd_done` should at least warn (or refuse without `--force`) when called on a job whose status is already `done`, the same defensive spirit as `decide.py rule` refusing a ruling with no defeater. This is likely to recur any time the same job gets dispatched to two concurrent agents (a real scenario per this batch's own "several of you running concurrently" framing).

lab_env.py's isolate() `also=` parameter assumes every extra (module, [attrs]) redirect target is a single FILE path: `fname = Path(str(current)).name if current else f"{attr}.json"` takes the current value's basename and redirects that one filename into the lab dir. This does not work for a DIRECTORY-valued global (e.g. nodes/inner_monologue_node.py's own _DATA_DIR, or core/memory_edges.py's/core/opponent_process.py's own _DATA, all `Path(__file__).parent.parent/"data"`, a whole directory, not one file) -- passing one of these to `also=` would redirect it to `<lab_dir>/data` and try to treat that as a FILE path, breaking any code that does `_DATA.mkdir(...)` or opens multiple different files under it. Hit this directly while scoping isolation for J-0643 (train_split_merge Step 2 replay lab, F-1006): several modules a lab script transitively touches (core.social_moves, core.memory_edges, core.opponent_process, nodes.inner_monologue_node itself) all key off a directory-valued _DATA/_DATA_DIR global rather than a single-file one, so `also=` could not cleanly redirect them even though the underlying Path(__file__)-relative pattern is otherwise exactly what `also=` is designed for. Worked around by relying on running from inside a git worktree instead (which isolates by giving every Path(__file__)-relative global its own physically separate worktree-local directory automatically) rather than by using `also=` for these specific modules. Consider: let `also=` accept a directory-valued attr (detected via `current.is_dir()` or a caller-supplied flag) and redirect it to `<lab_dir>/<attr_name>/` as a directory rather than assuming a single file.

lab_env.py's isolate() docstring (and the job-queue "isolation: required" boilerplate text that tells an agent to use it) is written entirely around the transitive-write case: a module that calls into core.memory.store underneath. It gives no guidance for the -- apparently recurring -- other case: a script that is ALREADY read-only by construction (sqlite3.connect(..., mode=ro) plus plain open() reads, no import of core.memory.store or any other Nascence application module at all), where isolate() is not just unnecessary but actively the wrong tool (it would require importing unrelated Nascence app code into a standalone analysis script just to satisfy the letter of the instruction, for zero added protection, since there is no transitive write path for its DB_PATH patch to guard). This exact judgment call has now been independently re-derived at least three times on the same du_lens_first_test.py / du_lens_test_c_docaudit.py family of scripts (J-0684, J-0685, and now J-0687 -- none of them call isolate(), each session presumably worked out why on its own) without ever being written down. Suggest adding one paragraph to lab_env.py's own docstring (and/or the job-queue SKILL.md's isolation-required section) naming this second case explicitly: when a script under test has NO import of core.memory.store or another live-write-capable module, and connects to nascence.db (if at all) via mode=ro, the isolation requirement is satisfied by that read-only connection itself plus the existing "check the live DB immediately after" backstop -- isolate() is for the transitive-write case specifically, not a blanket requirement for every isolation:required job regardless of whether the code under test can write at all.

lab_env.py's isolate() hardcodes _ROOT = Path(r"C:\Nascence") for BOTH _LAB_ROOT (data/_lab/<timestamp>)
and _LIVE_DB (data/memory/nascence.db), with no way to point it at a different worktree's own data/
dir. This job (J-0704) needed to verify a mechanism (core/profile.py's write fence) from inside an
isolated worktree (per the ground rules' own "test in your own scratchpad, never touch the shared
tree" discipline) and found that calling isolate() from worktree-driven code would still create its
lab directory under the REAL C:\Nascence\data\_lab\, not under the worktree's own data/ -- because
_LAB_ROOT is computed from the hardcoded _ROOT, not from wherever the calling code's own core.profile
module resolves to. It is non-destructive (only ever COPIES the real nascence.db, never modifies it,
and only ADDS a new dir under data/_lab/) but it does leave artifacts in the shared C:\Nascence tree
from a job that was otherwise entirely isolated to its own worktree, and (per the module's own
docstring) nothing ever auto-deletes those lab dirs -- so this quietly accumulates in the shared tree
across many agents/sessions that each think they're testing in isolation. Worth a parameter (or an
auto-detected root, e.g. deriving _ROOT from wherever core.profile itself resolves at call time,
similar to how these job-queue smoke tests already assert `Path(profile.__file__).resolve()` against
their own worktree) so isolate() can be pointed at -- or auto-detect -- a worktree's own data/ dir
instead of always writing into the one shared C:\Nascence\data\_lab\. Not fixed here (out of scope for
J-0704, which used a bespoke smoke-test script instead, matching J-0610/F-0995's own precedent) --
flagging per this repo's CLAUDE.md rule 5 (a rough edge noticed while doing other work gets suggested,
not silently fixed or dropped).

job_queue.py's `start`/`done` subcommands accept --session and pass it through to ct.log_event() (correctly attributing the live session_events.jsonl entry), but neither one writes that session value back onto the job record's own top-level "session" field -- that field is set once at record creation (job_queue.py add/spawn) and never updated afterward. Net effect: running `job_queue.py show J-XXXX` after start+done with --session J-0676 on both calls can still print "session": "J-0609" if J-0609 was the session that originally spawned the job -- easy to misread as "the wrong session id was recorded" when actually the field means "created/spawned by" not "last worked by." Noticed while closing out J-0676 (spawned by J-0609's finding F-0968): both start and done were called with --session J-0676 exactly as instructed, but the job record's own session field still reads J-0609 in the final `show` output. Not a bug in the sense of losing data -- session_events.jsonl has the real per-action attribution -- but the field name/semantics on the job record itself invite exactly this confusion. Possible fix: rename the field to something like "spawned_by_session" (matching what it actually tracks), or add a separate "last_session" field that start/done do update, so `show`'s output isn't ambiguous about which session most recently touched a job.

job_queue.py's stored `session` field on a job record is set once at creation (the spawning session, e.g. via `add`/`spawn`) and is never updated by `start`/`done` -- those two commands only pass `--session` through to the live session_events.jsonl log (`ct.log_event(..., session=a.session)`), not back onto the job record itself (job_queue.py cmd_start/cmd_done, ~lines 259-278). Concretely: J-0717's own `job_queue.py show J-0717` output still reads `"session": "J-0632"` (the session that spawned it as a follow-up) even after this session ran `start J-0717 --session J-0717` and `done J-0717 --session J-0717` to completion -- a future reader glancing at the job record alone would wrongly conclude J-0632's session did the actual J-0717 work, when the live event log (correctly) shows J-0717 as both the starter and finisher. Not a data-loss bug (the true attribution is recoverable from session_events.jsonl), but a display/schema inconsistency worth fixing: either rename the job-record field to something like `spawned_by_session` to stop implying "who worked this," or have cmd_start/cmd_done also write the acting session onto the record (e.g. a `worked_by` list, since more than one session can touch a job across start/done).

decide.py open's plan-slug validator only checks docs/plans/ and docs/staged/ for a matching file, so any --plan against a legacy top-level doc (e.g. docs/memory_levels_plan.md, which predates the plans/staged convention and has never been moved) fails with "not a real plan slug... Use --force" even though the file genuinely exists and is genuinely the right target -- --force's own help text ("open against a plan slug that doesn't resolve to a real file... creates an orphan node") reads as if it is bypassing a real problem, when for memory_levels_plan specifically it is not creating an orphan at all (dozens of prior decisions, e.g. D-0173/D-0124/D-0116/D-0092/D-0091/D-0167/D-0183, already share this exact slug and clearly resolve fine in practice). Two ideas: (1) have the validator also check docs/ directly (not just docs/plans/ and docs/staged/) before refusing, so legacy top-level plan docs don't need --force at all; or (2) if that's deliberately excluded, soften --force's own help text for the case where the slug already has existing decision/finding history (i.e. distinguish "a slug with zero history, likely a typo" from "a slug with an established paper trail sitting in a directory the validator doesn't scan" -- the latter is not really an orphan node and the current wording doesn't reflect that). Hit this today opening D-0184/D-0185 against memory_levels_plan; used --force since it was clearly the same established slug as D-0173 etc., but the friction (and the momentary "did I typo this?" doubt) would recur for every future decision on this specific plan doc until it's either moved into docs/plans/ or the validator is widened.

job_queue.py spawn and findings_log.py spawn-job both lack a --isolation flag (confirmed via --help on both: job_queue.py add HAS --isolation {none,required}, but job_queue.py spawn and findings_log.py spawn-job do not offer it at all). This means a job created either way structurally defaults to isolation="none" in its own JSON regardless of what the author writes in --briefing prose. Real instance: J-0722 (spawned via findings_log.py spawn-job F-1040 ... by J-0688) shows "isolation": "none" in job_queue.py show's JSON output, while its own briefing text says "Isolation required for the smoke test (per this plan's own precedent)." Suggest adding --isolation {none,required} to both `job_queue.py spawn` and `findings_log.py spawn-job`, mirroring `job_queue.py add`'s existing flag, so isolation requirements set by a finding/decision-spawned job are structural rather than prose-only.

Job briefings can go stale on a named decision's ruled/open status between when a job is SPAWNED (carrying forward prose like "D-0173 not ruled, do not rule it") and when it actually RUNS -- caught live in J-0731 (F-1073): D-0173 was ruled by the founder 2026-09-06T20:23:28 UTC, about 5 hours BEFORE J-0652 (the job that spawned J-0731) even committed the finding that named D-0173 "not ruled" in its own plan-doc bullet -- so the briefing text J-0731 received had inherited an already-stale premise from its own parent job, not just gone stale during J-0731's own queue wait. Suggest job-queue (or whichever tool authors "audit X per <job>'s own dossier"-style briefings, e.g. job-run/spawn-job) note, alongside S-0084's own fix, that a caller/dependency LIST cited from a prior job's dossier should be re-pulled (fresh udms_get_change_dossier or `python udms.py check`, cheap) rather than copy-pasted, whenever the job doing the citing is itself an audit/due-diligence job for that same target file -- the exact case where a stale list silently narrows the audit's real scope.

job-queue's --autonomy field only has two values, {ready, needs_input}, and "needs_input" reads as "needs a founder RULING/decision". J-0641 (source decision:D-0166, autonomy=ready) exposes a third real category this schema can't express: a job that is fully decided/GO-ruled and evidenced, where the actual execution step itself was already attempted and found to require a human's own hands on the command (a live-behaviour-changing action for Du, per D-0166/F-0900's own text) -- not because anything is still undecided. Filed "ready" the same as any other autonomous build job, J-0641 sat untouched for 3 days (2026-09-05 -> 2026-09-08) across at least one prior full job-run batch, because every autonomous session that picks it up correctly re-discovers the same block and (correctly) declines, but nothing about the job's own autonomy tag flags it as different from an ordinary ready job to a human skimming the queue for what still needs their own attention specifically. Suggest a third autonomy value (e.g. needs_hands, or reusing needs_input with a distinguishing sub-tag) so job-queue list/next can surface "decided and ready, but only a human can press this button" separately from "still needs a founder ruling" -- the two need genuinely different responses from whoever is triaging the queue. See J-0641/F-1114/D-0189 for the concrete case.

CLAUDE.md's own tool-for-fact table lists "Confirmed follow-up work" as `/job-queue add`/`spawn`, or `findings_log.py spawn-job` -- presented as two interchangeable options via "or". They are NOT interchangeable: `findings_log.py spawn-job <finding-id> --kind ... --title ...` both creates the job_queue entry AND appends the new job id to that finding's own `spawned_jobs` array; calling `job_queue.py spawn --kind ... --from finding:<id> --title ...` directly creates a fully valid, correctly-cross-referenced job (its own `source`/`spawned_from` fields correctly point at the finding) but does NOT update the finding's own `spawned_jobs` array, leaving an asymmetric link (findable from the job backward to the finding, but not enumerable forward from the finding). Hit this for real in J-0780 (F-1140 -> J-0792): I read the CLAUDE.md table, reasonably inferred `job_queue.py spawn --from finding:X` was an equally valid choice since it's listed as the FIRST of the two "or" options, and only noticed the gap afterward when F-1140's own `spawned_jobs` came back `[]`. Suggest either: (a) reword the CLAUDE.md table entry to make `findings_log.py spawn-job` the preferred/canonical path when the follow-up is spawned FROM a finding specifically (not job-queue's own generic `spawn --from`), or (b) teach `job_queue.py spawn --from finding:<id>` to also append the new job's id to that finding's own `spawned_jobs` array (mirroring what `findings_log.py spawn-job` already does), so the two paths produce an equivalent result regardless of which one a session reaches for.

job_run.py's _is_hold() heuristic (the literal-prefix "Hold" check S-0053 already flagged the false-negative side of) has a false-POSITIVE counterpart too: an ordinary ruling whose literal first word happens to be "Hold" in a normal-English sense ("Hold X steady", "Hold off on Y") -- not a founder execution-freeze marker -- gets misclassified as ACTIVE_HOLD. Hit this for real 2026-09-08: D-0183's own ruling text ("Hold -- leave keep=3500 fixed for now...") triggered ACTIVE_HOLD:D-0183 on the whole memory_levels_plan in job_run.py plan's output, even though the ruling is just a normal decided value, not a stop-all-work freeze. Fixed the immediate instance by re-wording the ruling to avoid the literal prefix, but the underlying detection gap (matching only a bare string prefix, no semantic distinction between "Hold [an execution freeze]" and "Hold [a value/course steady]") remains. Same root cause S-0053 already named: decide.py should support/encourage an explicit structured field (e.g. `--hold` flag on decide.py rule, or a `status: hold` field) instead of relying on ruling-text prefix conventions at all -- this suggestion is additional evidence for that same fix, from the opposite failure direction.

lab_env.py hardcodes _ROOT = Path(r"C:\Nascence") and its own isolate().__enter__() does sys.path.insert(0, str(_ROOT)) before patching core.memory.store.DB_PATH. This is safe when the calling script already runs from the live tree (ROOT already equals C:\Nascence), but is a real, currently-untested risk for a worktree-anchored lab script -- and this whole job-queue toolchain routinely dispatches jobs into throwaway git worktrees under a scratchpad path, not the live tree, per the job-run/job-queue ground rules. A worktree-anchored script's own ROOT (typically Path(__file__).parent.parent) is its OWN worktree root, already inserted at sys.path[0] before it imports anything from core/nodes. If that script later imports lab_env (which additionally inserts C:\Nascence at sys.path[0], ahead of the worktree root), any core.*/nodes.* submodule NOT YET imported by that point could resolve against the LIVE tree's copy instead of the worktree's own -- silently testing the wrong source for that one submodule while everything already-imported stays correctly worktree-scoped, since Python's sys.modules cache means only not-yet-imported names are at risk. This is distinct from S-0030/S-0033's own already-filed WAL-mode/shutil.copy2 DB-snapshot concern -- this one is about the sys.path side effect of importing the module at all, independent of what isolate() does internally once entered.

Concretely hit this on J-0791 (2026-09-08, train_split_merge plan): needed isolation for a worktree-anchored lab script whose Du-offline gate meant the live-call branch could not be exercised this session at all, so an import-order workaround could not even be tested before shipping it. Worked around by NOT importing lab_env for that script -- used a direct, import-free nascence.db mtime/size stat() check as the DB backstop instead (no sys.path mutation, no DB copy needed since the call path independently has zero core.memory.store reachability) -- but a future worktree-anchored job whose call path DOES need the DB_PATH redirect (not just a stat backstop) will hit this for real.

Two independent fixes, either would resolve it, not mutually exclusive: (1) have lab_env.py compute _ROOT from the actual live-tree marker (e.g. walk up from a known-fixed anchor, or accept a ROOT override argument to isolate()/the module-level functions) rather than hardcoding C:\Nascence, so a worktree-anchored caller can tell it "the live tree is over there, but resolve MY OWN core.* imports against my own worktree" -- OR (2) document the risk explicitly in lab_env.py's own module docstring (the "Usage" section) with the concrete mitigation (import every core.* submodule your script needs BEFORE importing lab_env, so they are already cached in sys.modules under the worktree's own path and the later sys.path reordering cannot affect them), so a future worktree-anchored job at least makes an informed choice instead of discovering this from scratch or copying an untested pattern.

J-0803 (2026-09-08, executing D-0184's live DB backfill half) hit a real, reproducible block: a direct write to data/memory/nascence.db (a fully dry-run-validated, 4-row UPDATE) was refused by this session's own Claude Code auto-mode permission classifier, identically via both the Bash and PowerShell tools ("Permission for this action was denied by the Claude Code auto mode classifier. Reason: Blocked by classifier."). No human was present in this batch dispatch to approve the prompt, and per this project's own discipline the block was not routed around.

Suggest job-run's (or job-queue's) own docs/briefing template note this explicitly: a job whose scope includes a live production-data write (an UPDATE/INSERT/DELETE against data/memory/nascence.db, or any equivalent live store) should either (a) be scoped from the start as two separate jobs -- a `ready`-autonomy investigate+dry-run job, and a `needs_input`-autonomy apply job for a session where the founder can actually approve the prompt or run the write directly -- or (b) be flagged in the job briefing itself that the write step may need to fall back to spawning a needs_input follow-up, so a batch-dispatched agent doesn't spend its whole run only to discover this at the very last step with nothing else to show. J-0803 happened to have a substantial code-fix half that was independent of the blocked write, so it wasn't left with nothing -- but a job whose ENTIRE scope is a single live write would be.

job_queue.py has no way to flip a job's autonomy (needs_input -> ready) or close it as declined/superseded once the founder answers: only add/spawn/list/next/show/start/done exist. decide.py needs a 'reslug' (or 'move') subcommand: decide.py reslug D-XXXX --to SLUG --session S --why "...". plan_maintain's decision-bad-slug job briefing currently tells the agent to hand-edit the "plan" field in docs/decisions.jsonl and then rerun plan_maintain.py -- both of which CLAUDE.md and the job-run ground rules forbid (never hand-edit a .jsonl store; never run plan_maintain.py from a batch agent), so J-0856/J-0857-style jobs cannot be completed as briefed. The command should: (1) refuse unless plan_exists(new slug) (or --force), (2) rewrite under ct.locked(STORE) + save(), (3) pop the awaits_decision/decided_by edges keyed on the OLD slug before calling sync_edges(rec) -- sync_edges only pops edges keyed on rec["plan"], i.e. the NEW slug, so a plain reslug+sync would leave a stale plan:<old>->decision edge in _memory_edges.jsonl, (4) append a history entry recording old slug/why/session, (5) log_event kind=decision_reslugged. Then update plan_maintain.py's decision-bad-slug briefing text (lines ~207-217) to point at the new command instead of a hand edit + full rebuild. A ready-to-adapt reference implementation of steps 2-3 and 5 is in scratchpad reslug_D-0194_J-0856.py.

Two rough edges surfaced by J-0857 (D-0198 'toolchain_ops') and its sibling J-0856 (D-0194 'local_tier_ops'): (1) decide.py open --force lets a toolchain/ops ruling with no Du plan be filed under an invented pseudo-slug, and plan_maintain then auto-files a decision-bad-slug job for it on every run -- a round trip that ends in an agent hand-nulling the field. Give non-plan decisions a sanctioned representation instead: e.g. accept --plan none (stored as null, already what lint skips and what D-0013/J-0053 and now D-0198 use), or a small reserved set of ops pseudo-slugs the lint treats as valid, so --force stops being the only path. (2) decide.sync_edges pops stale awaits_decision/decided_by edges keyed on rec['plan'] AFTER the plan field changed, so a slug correction always leaves the old plan-keyed edge behind (D-0013 still carries a stale plan:factory_stations awaits_decision edge from 2026-08-23; J-0857 had to pop toolchain_ops explicitly). Pop by dst_id=D-xxxx + edge_type only, without the src_id filter, and add a decide.py set-plan subcommand so the briefing's 'hand-edit the JSONL line' step goes away.

plan_snapshot.py report classifies a plan as 'stalled' purely from days since the (stage_word, open_decisions, worst_liveness) tuple last changed (classify(), lines ~331-357, STALLED_DAYS=30). A plan that reached its terminal healthy stage and stays there — identity_estate has been 🟢 LIVE since 08-15 with a shadow log written within the hour — reads '🕸 stalled, last change 2026-07-06' forever, indistinguishable from a genuinely abandoned plan. J-0853 (2026-09-09 stalled-plan review) was spawned on exactly that misreading. Suggest: (a) fold the plan's '## Current State — verified YYYY-MM-DD' date (plan_liveness already parses it as VERIFIED_RE) into the change signal, so a fresh verification counts as movement; and/or (b) exempt stages LIVE/SHIPPED/SUPERSEDED/DEAD from the stalled verdict the way plan_index.py:436 already exempts SHIPPED/SUPERSEDED from its stale marker, reporting them as 'steady' instead. Either way the report should say WHICH signal was silent (stage vs verification vs evidence mtime) rather than one word.

`decide.py open`'s plan_exists() check (decide.py line 70-71: `any((d / f"{slug}.md").exists() for d in PLANS_DIRS)`) only checks docs/plans/ and docs/staged/ -- it does not check bare docs/<slug>.md. memory_levels_plan.md (this whole plan's own doc, ~1994 lines, Phase 0+1 explicitly marked BUILT & LIVE, dozens of decisions and jobs already filed under this exact slug) lives directly at C:\Nascence\docs\memory_levels_plan.md, not under docs/plans/ or docs/staged/ -- confirmed by direct filesystem check 2026-09-12 (J-0826), both in the live tree and in a job-run worktree. This means `decide.py open --plan memory_levels_plan` fails plan_exists() and demands --force every single time for this specific plan, unconditionally -- discovered when J-0826's own `decide.py open` call hit exactly this ("'memory_levels_plan' is not a real plan slug (checked docs/plans/ and docs/staged/)"), worked around with --force per the tool's own suggested escape hatch. Two independent fixes worth considering, not conflated: (1) decide.py's plan_exists() (and presumably plan-index/plan-files-audit/plan-liveness, if they use the same PLANS_DIRS convention) could also check a bare docs/<slug>.md so a legacy-location plan doesn't need --force forever; (2) per this project's OWN CLAUDE.md convention #3 ("a plan that's live goes in docs/plans/... move the file when it graduates; don't invent a third bucket"), memory_levels_plan.md itself is long overdue to move from docs/ into docs/plans/ (it has said "BUILT & LIVE" in its own Status line since well before 2026-08-23's docs/plans+docs/staged convention existed) -- not done here since moving this specific, heavily-cross-referenced file is a real change with its own blast radius (memory-links harvesting, ROADMAP.md links, other plans' cross-references), not a side effect of an unrelated watch-chain job.

Neither job_queue.py spawn nor findings_log.py spawn-job exposes an --isolation flag, even though job_queue's own JSON schema carries an isolation field (seen on J-0827 itself: isolation="required", which is what forced this job to route every reproduction through lab_env.isolate() with a live-file backstop). A job spawned via either CLI today always gets whatever the default is (observed "none" on J-0908, spawned from findings_log.py spawn-job) regardless of how load-bearing that need is in the job's own free-text briefing. J-0908 (this job's own spawn, F-1270) is exactly the case where this matters: it is a job about a live-data write-fence bypass, whose own fix and verification MUST be isolated the same way J-0827 was, but the only place that requirement lives today is a sentence inside --briefing/--briefing-file text, not the structured field a future job-queue listing/filter could act on (e.g. job-queue next / job-run's own tiering, or a future "list every isolation=required job" query). Suggest adding --isolation {required,none} (or similar) to both spawn commands, defaulting to none to match today's behavior for everything else.

J-0834 (train_split_merge, F-1271) hit a real UnicodeEncodeError ('charmap' codec, position ~111-112, a macron in "pīwakawaka") when a fresh lab script printed a real judge why-text to a redirected stdout file -- the exact, already-documented feedback_windows_charmap_daemons.md convention ("every script needs sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding='utf-8')"), but this convention lives only in a Claude memory file, not in lab_env.py's own module docstring or usage example, and lab_env.py is specifically the module every isolation-required lab script in this toolchain is told to import. A lab script that calls real judge_panel/model_client endpoints and prints their output (why-text, generated thoughts, claim text) is exactly the shape of script most likely to hit this -- real generated text routinely contains accented names, macrons, curly quotes, em dashes. Suggest adding one line to lab_env.py's own module docstring (or its "Usage" section) noting this gotcha and the one-line fix, right next to the existing `isolate()` usage example, so a future session writing a NEW lab script from that docstring's own template sees it before hitting the crash rather than after (this session lost ~1 minute of real live-infra call time re-doing the crashed portion, harmless here but would be worse on a longer/more expensive real-infra batch). Not urgent, not blocking -- a documentation-only addition to an existing skill file.

job_queue.py's `autonomy: needs_input` field is set once at job creation (job_queue.py spawn --from decision:D-XXXX) and never re-evaluated. Confirmed live 2026-09-12: J-0881 was spawned from decision:D-0207 with autonomy=needs_input and a briefing that says "waits on D-0207 ruling B or C"; D-0207 was just ruled (B) via /decide-review, but `job_queue.py list --plan peer_correspondence_plan` still shows J-0881 flagged needs-input afterward -- the flag did not clear. lab_env.py's isolate() context manager (D-0206/J-0911's own new auto-delete-unwritten-DB-copy feature, added 2026-09-12) has an intermittent Windows file-locking bug: across two separate python.exe invocations minutes apart in the same job (J-0910), each doing `with lab_env.isolate(db="empty") as lab_dir: <a handful of real awaited network calls, no DB access at all>`, the first call's __exit__ succeeded cleanly ("[lab_env] restored 1 redirected global(s)" printed normally) but the second raised `PermissionError: [WinError 32] The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process` on `self._db_path.unlink()` -- the identical code path, same machine, same isolate(db="empty") call shape. Likely cause: SQLite's own file handle from `_store.init_db()` (called inside __enter__ when db="empty") is not always released by the time __exit__'s own hash-and-unlink check runs, a real Windows-specific race (POSIX generally allows deleting an open file; Windows does not). Impact when it fires: the exception propagates out of the `with` block BEFORE the patched globals (module, attr, original) get restored in the `for module, attr, original in reversed(self._patches): setattr(...)` loop below the unlink() call -- so a caller whose own code after the `with` block still expected the isolation redirect (or expected core.memory.store.DB_PATH to be restored to live) could be surprised; in my own case this only cost losing the auto-write of a results JSONL file and an automatic canary snapshot (both real data was already collected and printed before the crash, so nothing was lost, just had to be reconstructed by hand from stdout). Suggested fix: wrap the `self._db_path.unlink()` call in its own try/except (log-and-continue on a PermissionError specifically, same as the pattern this file already uses elsewhere for non-fatal cleanup), OR move the patch-restoration loop BEFORE the delete-unwritten-copy check so a crash in the optional cleanup optimization can never prevent the mandatory global-restoration step. Reproduction: two back-to-back scripts in the same job, each doing `with lab_env.isolate(db="empty") as lab_dir: <a handful of real awaited network calls, no DB access at all>` -- first call's __exit__ succeeded, second (a separate python.exe invocation, not the same process) failed. Not reliably reproducible on demand (this is the only occurrence observed so far, out of 3 isolate() calls this session), consistent with a timing race rather than a deterministic bug. Full context: findings-log F-1280 (job J-0910, plan train_split_merge).

see scripts/_test_practical_lesson.py, scripts/lane2_canary_harness.py), this pushes C:\Nascence
ahead of the calling worktree's own earlier sys.path.insert(0, <worktree root>), so core.* silently
resolves from C:\Nascence's live tree instead of the worktree being tested -- confirmed empirically

plain from a worktree, and only resolved to the worktree's own copy once PYTHONPATH=C:\Nascence was

skip the insert). This did not change today's specific verdict (both copies happened to carry the fix
under test), but it means any prior isolation="required" job that ran a lab_env-isolated test script
from its own worktree without realizing this may have silently verified C:\Nascence's live code
instead of its own worktree's edits. Suggest either: (a) lab_env.py's own docstring/module comment
names this explicitly, with the PYTHONPATH=C:\Nascence workaround, so a job doesn't have to
rediscover it; or (b) lab_env.py checks sys.path for an existing worktree-shaped core/ package before

lab_env.py: `isolate(db="empty")` reliably raises `PermissionError: [WinError 32] The process cannot
access the file because it is being used by another process` inside `__exit__`'s own D-0206
auto-delete-if-unwritten step (`self._db_path.unlink()`), on this Windows machine, because
`core.memory.store.init_db()` leaves the freshly-created sqlite file handle open. Worse: because that
unlink() raises, the `for module, attr, original in reversed(self._patches): setattr(...)` restore
loop right below it in the same `__exit__` method never runs either -- so on this failure path
`core.memory.store.DB_PATH` (and anything else passed via `also=`) stays patched to the (deleted-
attempt-failed) lab-dir path for the rest of the process instead of being restored to live. Reproduced
twice (verify_J-0876.py, job J-0876/F-1291, 2026-09-12) with a no-op call
(`InnerMonologueNode`/`core.frontier` calls that never touch the DB at all) -- both times left a
stray never-written `nascence.db` under `C:\Nascence\data\_lab\<timestamp>\` (harmless: inside the
write-fence's own allow-listed _lab subtree, subject to retention.py's 14-day uncited-dir
quarantine). Switching to `db="copy"` (default) avoided it both times, since it never opens a
connection against the lab copy when the code under test doesn't touch the DB. Possible fixes: (1)
`init_db()` should close its own connection/dispose its handle before returning; (2) `__exit__`
should restore the patches in a `finally` block (or before attempting the unlink), so a failed
cleanup-delete can never also skip the more important patch-restoration; (3) wrap the unlink() itself
in a narrow try/except so a locked file just gets left for the existing retention sweep instead of
raising out of `__exit__`.

job_queue.py has no way to revert an in_progress job back to open. Its own state machine (job_queue.py lines ~226-227, ~263, ~274) only supports open -> in_progress (start) -> done (done); cmd_next only ever selects status == "open", so once start has run, that job id is permanently invisible to `next`/`list --ready` even if it is never finished. This collided directly with J-0880: its own briefing (a gate-check job meant to be re-picked-up later if a data gate isn't yet met) says "if the gate is not met, say so with the real row counts and leave the job open" -- but the Tier-3 job-run dispatch template calls `start` unconditionally as step 2, before the gate can even be checked (checking it is step 3+). Once started, there is no CLI verb to put it back to "open" short of hand-editing job_queue.jsonl, which CLAUDE.md explicitly forbids. Result: J-0880 sits at in_progress/done_at=null after this session -- accurately reflecting that someone looked and the gate wasn't met, but invisible to future `next`/`list --ready` scans, so nothing will naturally re-surface it once the gate is met later. Worth adding something like a `job_queue.py defer <id>` (or `reopen`) verb that resets status to open (optionally bumping created/adding a "not-before" date field cmd_next could respect), for this exact recurring shape of job: a gated re-check that should stay pickable rather than spawning a fresh job id every cycle (contrast the older Buddha/marcus cadence-check jobs, J-0185->J-0186->J-0204->..., which worked around the same gap by spawning a new job id each time and marking the old one done).

lab_env.py's isolate().__exit__ (D-0206's auto-delete-if-unwritten path, added J-0911) calls self._db_path.unlink() with NO try/except around it. On a real run (J-0885, 2026-09-14, C:\Nascence\data\_lab\20260914_120603\nascence.db) this raised PermissionError ([WinError 32] The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process) even though the copy WAS genuinely unwritten (every call the script made against DB_PATH across ~300 _connect() calls was a SELECT, confirmed by reading every function called: get_shadow_events/get_light_events_by_source/get_event_sources/get_resolution_drain, plus 4 ad hoc COUNT(*) queries, all via sqlite3.connect+.close()). The unhandled exception killed the whole calling script AFTER it had already finished all its real work and written its own results to disk -- i.e. a best-effort cleanup step (the unlink is explicitly framed in the docstring as an optimization, not a correctness requirement) turned a fully successful run into a crashed one from the caller's point of view, and left the 683 MB copy sitting on disk exactly like an ordinary "kept" lab dir even though it should have auto-deleted.

Manually confirmed the lock was transient/process-local, not a real leak: retried `Remove-Item -LiteralPath <same path> -Force` a few seconds later, AFTER the crashed Python process had fully exited, and it succeeded immediately. Most likely mechanism (not independently proven, but consistent with everything observed): one or more sqlite3.Connection objects from the run's many `with _connect() as conn:` blocks (note: `with` on a sqlite3.Connection only commits/rolls back in __exit__, it does NOT close the connection -- closing happens only via CPython refcounting once the local `conn` var goes out of scope) had not yet had their OS-level file handle/WAL mmap released by Windows at the exact moment __exit__'s own unlink() ran in that same process, even though nothing in Python-land was still holding a live reference.

Suggested fix: wrap the `self._db_path.unlink()` call (lab_env.py, isolate.__exit__, the D-0206 block) in try/except OSError (or the narrower PermissionError) and fall back to the existing "kept, left for inspection" behaviour on failure -- exactly what already happens today when the hash check finds the copy WAS written to. That keeps the optimization for the common case, degrades gracefully to today's pre-D-0206 behaviour on the rare Windows-timing case instead of crashing an otherwise-successful caller, and costs nothing else (retention.py's existing 14-day-uncited window still reclaims it either way). A one-line print noting the fallback (e.g. "[lab_env] DB copy unlink failed transiently, left for inspection: <err>") would make this self-diagnosing the way the rest of the module already is, without needing a caller to notice by hand the way J-0885 did.

isolate().__exit__'s D-0206 auto-delete-if-unwritten check can raise PermissionError on Windows: a plain read-only dry-run (core.memory.store.prune_episodic(dry_run=True), which only ever does `with _connect() as conn: ... SELECT ...`) left the sqlite3 connection apparently still holding a Windows file lock on lab_dir/nascence.db by the time __exit__ tried self._db_path.unlink() (byte-identical, so D-0206 correctly wanted to delete it) -- reproduced twice in a row, same traceback, WinError 32 "The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process". Net effect: the full ~650MB DB copy is silently left on disk instead of being cleaned up (harmless -- scripts/retention.py's existing labs-class windows still catch it eventually -- but it defeats the whole point of D-0206's optimization for every caller that hits this, and the raised exception itself can crash a caller's own script if it isn't wrapped in try/except, which is not obvious from the docstring). _connect()'s own `with _connect() as conn:` pattern only commits/rolls back a sqlite3.Connection as a context manager, it does NOT close() it -- CPython refcounting usually closes it promptly once `conn` goes out of scope, but that's evidently not reliable enough on Windows to guarantee __exit__'s unlink() succeeds right after prune_episodic() returns. Possible fixes worth considering (not evaluated here, just flagged): __exit__ could retry-with-backoff around the unlink (Windows file locks are often momentarily held by antivirus/indexing too), or gc.collect() before the hash+unlink attempt, or __exit__ could catch PermissionError itself and log a warning instead of letting it propagate (matching D-0206's own "left exactly as before" fallback for the changed-DB case). Found incidentally by J-0905 while running its own required isolated dry-run (scratchpad/isolated_dryrun_J-0905.py) -- worked around in that job's own script by writing a checkpoint file before the `with isolate()` block's __exit__ runs, not by touching lab_env.py itself.

lab_env.py's isolate(db="empty") D-0206 auto-delete crashes on Windows when nothing ever writes through the redirected DB_PATH: __exit__ calls self._db_path.unlink() after confirming the hash is unchanged, but core.memory.store.init_db()'s own sqlite3 connection appears to still hold an OS-level lock on the file at that point, so unlink() raises PermissionError ("[WinError 32] The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process") instead of quietly deleting it. Hit twice in this same session (J-0920, 2026-09-14) using isolate(also=[...], db="empty") from a standalone script -- both times every other line of the `with` block had already run and printed correctly, and the crash only happened at __exit__ itself, after the block's own work was done, so it did not lose data here, but it does mean the context manager itself raises instead of returning cleanly, and a caller that puts a `return` or further cleanup inside the `with` block, or that relies on the block exiting without an exception, would be surprised by this. The lab dir and its unwritten nascence.db are left behind either way (matches the documented pre-D-0206 fallback), so the only real defect is the unhandled exception itself, not data loss. Suggested fix: either have init_db() explicitly close its own sqlite3 connection before returning (POSIX would tolerate the open handle at unlink time; Windows will not), or wrap the D-0206 unlink() in __exit__ in a try/except so a locked file just falls back to "left on disk for inspection" instead of crashing the whole context manager -- matching the already-tolerant spirit of the surrounding code (a changed-hash DB copy is already just "left exactly as before", not treated as an error).

lab_env.py's _new_lab_dir() names dirs via time.strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S") (1-second granularity) with mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) -- confirmed today (J-0915, 2026-09-14) that two isolate() calls landing in the same wall-clock second silently REUSE the same directory rather than erroring: reproduced twice, back-to-back, in a single fast job-scoped verify script (two isolate(db="empty") blocks in one process both resolved to the identical timestamped dir, e.g. C:\Nascence\data\_lab\20260914_164308 used for both).

Within one script/process that's probably harmless (sequential, no concurrent write). But this project routinely runs MANY concurrent Tier-3 job-run agents at once, each with its own isolate() calls against the SAME shared C:\Nascence\data\_lab\ root -- two DIFFERENT PROCESSES colliding on the same lab dir within the same second would mean both setting core.memory.store.DB_PATH to files in the SAME directory concurrently: one's shutil.copy2()/init_db(), its _hash_file() baseline capture, and its eventual unlink()-or-keep decision at exit could all race against the other's on the identical file. That is a real, previously-undiscovered silent cross-contamination risk between two unrelated concurrent agents' supposedly-isolated runs, not just a cosmetic directory-naming collision -- worse than the DB-copy-unlink issue this job (F-1279/J-0915) actually fixed, if it is ever hit in practice.

Not investigated further here -- out of this job's own scope (J-0915 was about the unlink() PermissionError specifically). Suggest: give _new_lab_dir() a real uniqueness guard -- e.g. append a sub-second component or the PID, or retry with mkdir(exist_ok=False) on collision -- rather than relying on 1-second granularity being fine enough for concurrent agents sharing one lab root.

Secondary, smaller finding from the same job (see F-1372 in findings-log for full evidence): `git commit -- <pathspec>` does NOT commit a hand-staged index entry for that path -- it reads the CURRENT WORKING TREE content instead, silently discarding a `git hash-object` + `git update-index --cacheinfo` surgical stage built specifically to avoid sweeping in other agents' concurrent uncommitted writes. Worth a line in this project's CLAUDE.md's own "never git stash/reset/checkout--/restore in the shared tree" section (or a new project-tooling doc) since the exact "stage by exact hunk, then commit -- <path>" pattern several of this leak's own prior fix-jobs (and this job's own briefing) recommend is NOT safe against this gotcha as written -- the correct incantation to actually commit a hand-staged index without touching the working tree is `git commit --no-verify -- ` is NOT it either; the safe form is to omit the trailing pathspec entirely once the index has been surgically prepared with ONLY the intended change staged (verified via `git diff --cached` before committing), i.e. a plain `git commit -m ...` with no path arguments once the index is known-correct -- or, more robustly, `git commit -m ... --only -- <path>` which per git's own docs DOES commit the staged index content for that path rather than the working tree (untested this session, worth verifying before relying on it).

J-0951 (train_split_merge) was queued 2026-09-13T21:09 explicitly to prep a characterization battery for "whichever way the founder's fresh read on D-0213 goes." By the time a Tier-3 job-run dispatch picked it up (2026-09-15), D-0213 had already been ruled twice more (2026-09-14T03:24 by travis, then 2026-09-14T04:49 by claude per a fired defeater) and its own resolution -- a conservative UNDETERMINED fallback -- had already been built AND live-verified in code (J-0986/F-1369), fully superseding the schema-characterization direction J-0951 was meant to inform.

text: du_restart_history.py's live_process_start() has a real self-match bug: its own PowerShell invocation is built as "Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Where-Object { $_.CommandLine -match [regex]::Escape('run_nascence.py') } | ..." -- that command string literally contains the substring "run_nascence.py" inside the search pattern itself, so the WMI query matches its OWN powershell.exe subprocess (whose CommandLine is exactly that -Command text) every single time it runs, regardless of whether a real run_nascence.py process exists. Fix idea: build the search substring outside the -Command string (e.g. pass it as a -Command argument via a separate variable/parameter, or filter client-side in Python on the returned CommandLine field after a broad Win32_Process dump, or exclude PID == the subprocess's own PID / processes named powershell.exe) so the query text itself never contains the literal string it's searching for.

Root cause of the false GATE-MET verdicts already reported in S-0038 / S-0099, found 2026-09-19 (see findings log entry for this session): plan_liveness.py line 84's second THRESHOLD_RES pattern captures (\d+) with no number-boundary guard, so "25,475+ rows" -> 475 and "14,210+ rows" -> 210 (live on idle_executive_plan, geometry_tuple_index, the_consciousness_program). Suggest: (1) prefix every numeric capture with a lookbehind such as (?<![\d,.]) and allow an optional thousands-separated form so "14,210" parses as 14210 (which is then correctly ignored as a description of a large existing log); (2) accept the trailing-plus form only inside a target-framed sentence (needs / until / once / bar / gate / threshold in the same sentence), because descriptive "N+ rows" ("mid-flight on 575+ rows", "~400+ rows created within the same half-second") cannot be told apart from a target by the number alone; (3) stop applying one plan-level threshold to every evidence file the plan claims: require the sentence to name the log, else print "-" so GATE-MET cannot fire. Complements S-0038 (exclude docs/*.jsonl stores) and S-0099 (defeater-evidence field).

text: Hand-off hazard found landing J-1041 (2026-09-19, F-1559): when a blocked patch is handed to a later job as a full-file "drop-in replacement" embedded in the briefing, the live file can move before anyone lands it, and a verbatim replace then silently reverts the intervening change. Here J-1017 embedded its whole job_run.py at ~13:11 NZST on 2026-09-15; J-1016 landed file_overlaps root= and _plan_doc_repr() into the same file at 14:34; J-1041's "byte-for-byte replace" would have deleted J-1016's work with no error anywhere. Caught only because the landing session diffed live against the embedded file first. Suggest: (1) a blocked-patch hand-off should carry a unified diff (or the specific hunks) plus the base file's hash/mtime, not the full file; (2) the job-run/job-queue runbook should say "before landing any embedded file, diff it against the live file and apply only the hunks that are the job's own" and "if the live file has changed since the base, three-way merge"; (3) a landing session should keep a pre-edit backup and re-diff afterwards.

text: job_run.py's STALE-LOOKING IN-PROGRESS section ranks waiting jobs by calendar age only, so it cannot tell cumulative-live-runtime gates (most of the restart-gated ones) from genuinely contiguous-run gates, and every reader has to re-derive live time from data/nascence.log by hand. 2026-09-21 tally (parsing the awake/shutdown lines): since 2026-08-28 Du accrued 15.9 live-days across 24.5 calendar days (65 percent uptime; longest single run 61.1 h), and since the cat_overhaul merge commit 2261ca9 it accrued 7.37 live-days over 9 runs even though no run exceeded 2.1 days. Calendar age therefore badly understates how many "wait a week after restart" jobs have actually cleared. Suggest: add live-hours-since-started to each STALE line, and, when the briefing names a commit, live-hours since the first restart onto it. Prototype that already works: scratchpad live_since.py (takes a commit-ish or a local time; prints each run since the first restart at/after it, cumulative live hours, longest run). It should live next to job_run.py or in _plan_tools_common so plan-liveness and job-queue can share it. Also worth stating in job-queue SKILL.md: prefer wording a gate as "N live-days on commit X" so it is machine-checkable.

job-queue has no machine-readable gate for restart-gated jobs. J-0638 (created 2026-09-05) waited on "a restart onto commit c6b9cd3" written only in its briefing prose; the gate actually opened at 2026-09-08 16:42 NZ, but nothing re-checked it, so the job sat in_progress for 12.9 days until a manual wave-1 reader (F-1608) found the gate already satisfied and 110 post-restart template thoughts waiting to be read. Suggest an optional gate field on add/spawn, for example --gate-restart-after COMMIT (optionally with --gate-live-hours N for genuinely cumulative waits), and have `job-queue next` / `job-run` evaluate it with the same logic as the wave-1 helper live_since.py (nascence.log "Nascence is awake" lines vs the commit's committer date; count only runs that START at or after it). A satisfied gate would then surface the job as ready, and an unmet one would show as waiting with the live-hours still remaining, instead of every reader re-deriving it from nascence.log by hand. Evidence that most such waits are event or cumulative rather than contiguous: F-1608 (this gate was one restart, satisfied 12.9 days earlier; the fix was exercised across 6 different runs).

job_queue.py has no way to annotate an existing job (no note/update subcommand; only add, spawn, list, next, show, start, done). A reader who reads an in_progress evidence-wait job and finds its briefing premise wrong or superseded (J-1026 2026-09-21: the briefing says the re-check needs a Du-offline lab dry-run, but F-1646 shows the tick log plus one read-only indexed query re-derives every number online) cannot attach the finding ids or a 'do not wait for this' pointer to the job itself. The next person who runs job_queue.py show or next on it sees the stale briefing and may wait for a lab window that no longer matters; the only carriers are the plan doc and the findings ledger. Suggest a `note` subcommand (append a dated, attributed line to the job record, printed by show and next, with --session) or an `amend-briefing` that keeps the original text and appends the revision, so an in_progress job can carry its own current state.

findings_log.py has only record / spawn-job / list / show, so a wording slip in an already-recorded claim can only be corrected by appending a second, corrective finding (J-1085 had to record F-1649 to correct one phrase in F-1648: it said 'exactly one line between' where the log has no line between). Consider an 'amend' or 'correct' subcommand that appends a linked correction record (keeping the original immutable and the ledger append-only, like the rest of the toolchain) and shows the correction inline in 'show' and 'list', so a reader of F-1648 sees F-1649 without knowing to look for it. A cheaper alternative is a required 'reread the claim once before record' hint in SKILL.md, since a long claim is written before it is recorded and there is no second chance.
